explanation:
## Size and capacity are different numbers

```cpp
std::vector<int> store;      // store.size() is the CAPACITY
std::size_t count{ 0 };      // count is the SIZE
```

Using a vector as the raw block is a convenience so the problem is about the
growth policy rather than about `new` and `delete`. Conceptually `store` is a
`int*` plus a length, and in real code the fields are exactly:

```cpp
int* data;            // the allocation
std::size_t size;     // how many are constructed and live
std::size_t cap;      // how many fit
```

with the invariant `size <= cap` holding at every moment. Everything a vector
does follows from maintaining it.

## Push

```cpp
if (count == store.size())
{
    std::size_t next{ store.size() == 0 ? 1 : store.size() * 2 };
    std::vector<int> bigger(next, 0);
    for (std::size_t j = 0; j < count; ++j) bigger[j] = store[j];
    store = bigger;
    ++grows;
}
store[count] = x;
++count;
```

Grow **before** storing, which is what makes `store[count] = x` unconditionally
safe on the line after. Four steps in the growth: allocate, copy, replace,
count it.

The `capacity == 0` special case is needed because doubling zero is zero -
`0 * 2` is 0, the storage never grows, and the next `store[count]` is out of
range. Every real vector has this case, which is why `std::vector` grows 0 to 1
and not 0 to 0.

## The sum that makes doubling worth it

Push n elements from empty. Growths happen when the size reaches 1, 2, 4, 8, ...
up to the last power of two at or below n, and each growth copies as many
elements as the old capacity held:

```
grow to 1:  copy 0        grow to 8:  copy 4
grow to 2:  copy 1        grow to 16: copy 8
grow to 4:  copy 2        ...
```

Total copies = 0 + 1 + 2 + 4 + ... + n/2 < n. So n pushes do fewer than n copies
*in total*, plus n writes for the elements themselves: **O(1) amortised per
push**, with about log2(n) reallocations overall.

Now grow by a fixed amount, say one slot per push:

```
push 1: copy 0      push 2: copy 1      push 3: copy 2   ...   push n: copy n-1
```

Total = 0 + 1 + ... + (n-1) = n(n-1)/2 = **O(n^2)**. For a million pushes that is
5 x 10^11 copies rather than 10^6. The difference between the two policies is
not a constant factor; it is a different complexity class, and it is the whole
content of CLRS chapter 17.4.

"Amortised O(1)" means the *total* over n operations is O(n), so the average is
constant - not that each one is fast. One particular push can copy a million
elements. That distinction matters in real systems: a server with a latency
budget per request cannot absorb the occasional O(n) push, which is why
latency-sensitive code calls `reserve()` up front and gets O(1) **worst case**
instead of amortised.

## Why 2, and why the real ones differ

Any constant factor greater than 1 gives amortised O(1); the factor only changes
the constants. Growth factor 1.5 wastes less memory - at most 50% over the live
size rather than 100% - and, more subtly, can reuse freed blocks: with doubling,
the sum of all previously freed blocks is always just under the size of the next
request, so the allocator can never satisfy it from the gap left behind. With
1.5 it eventually can.

So the implementations disagree:

| | growth factor |
| --- | --- |
| libstdc++ (GCC) | 2 |
| libc++ (Clang) | 2 |
| MSVC | 1.5 |

The standard specifies neither. It only requires `push_back` to be amortised
O(1), which pins the policy down to "geometric" and leaves the factor free.

## Popping does not shrink

`pop` only decrements `count`. The capacity stays, which is why the hidden case
that drains two elements and pushes again reports `grows 2` and not 3 - the
storage was still there.

That is deliberate in real vectors too. Shrinking on pop would make a
push/pop/push/push/pop pattern reallocate repeatedly, turning O(1) amortised
into O(n) per operation - the same trap as linear growth, arrived at from the
other direction. `std::vector` therefore never shrinks on its own; releasing the
memory is an explicit `shrink_to_fit()`, and even that is only a request.

## The index check that catches a negative

```cpp
long long idx{};
std::cin >> idx;
if (idx < 0 || idx >= static_cast<long long>(count)) { range; }
```

Two traps in one line.

**`idx >= count` with a signed `idx` and unsigned `count`** converts `idx` to
unsigned first - the usual arithmetic conversions prefer the unsigned type at
equal rank - so `-1` becomes 18446744073709551615 and compares as *greater* than
`count`. Here that happens to give the right verdict by luck. The dangerous
shape is the opposite test, `if (idx < count) use it;`, where `-1` passes the
check and then indexes with a huge value. `-Wsign-compare` warns about exactly
this, and it is part of `-Wall`.

**`idx >= count` rather than `idx > count`** - index `count` is one past the last
element. Those bytes exist, since `count <= capacity`, so reading them does not
crash and returns whatever is there. That is the quietest kind of out-of-range
read: no fault, no wrong-looking value, just data that was never put there.

AddressSanitizer catches it anyway. It knows the difference between a vector's
size and its capacity, and reports reading the gap as a
`container-overflow` - which is why these problems can be run under the
`sanitize` profile and have the mistake named rather than guessed at.

## What the user cannot see, and what breaks because of it

Capacity is invisible through the interface - the only way to notice it is the
cost of a push. But a reallocation has a consequence that is very visible:

```cpp
std::vector<int> v{ 1, 2, 3 };
int* p = &v[0];        // points into the current allocation
v.push_back(4);        // may reallocate: new block, old block freed
*p = 99;               // use-after-free if it did
```

Every pointer, reference and iterator into a vector is invalidated by any
operation that may reallocate - `push_back`, `insert`, `resize`, `reserve`. The
rule is in the standard, and the symptom without a sanitizer is a value that
changes for no reason, or a crash somewhere unrelated.

`reserve()` up front is the fix when you know the size, and it is the one that
also removes the amortised spike:

```cpp
std::vector<int> v;
v.reserve(1000);       // one allocation; no growth, no invalidation
```

This is the reason to have written the growth by hand once. "May reallocate" is
abstract until you have been the one freeing the old block.
